pedagogy.summary:
• Age/Topic: 11–12 — order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a number line; use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations.
• Standards—UK (DfE NC Mathematics, KS3): 'order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions; use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.'
• Standards—US (CCSS-M): 6.NS.C.7 — understand ordering and absolute value of rational numbers; write, interpret and explain statements of order (e.g. −3 > −7).
• Operational details: Order by POSITION on the number line (left = less), which handles negatives and mixed forms uniformly. Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) or place each on the line before applying symbols. Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ alongside <, >, = and distinguish strict from inclusive. Interpret order statements in context ('−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer').
• Checkpoint — Tier A (age 11): 'True or false: −5 < −2.' Tier B: 'Order 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, 7/10.' Tier C: 'Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.'
bestPractices: Order by position on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule, not sign-specific tricks
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤)
Read comparison statements aloud in context ('−3 is greater than −7 because it is warmer / further right')
Bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error deliberately with negatives (−5 vs −2) and unequal-length decimals
keyRepresentations: Number line as the arbiter of order (left → right = least → greatest)
Common-form conversion (3/4 → 0.75) to compare across representations
Symbol cards =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ placed between two values
Sorting track / ordering slots that snap items into line positions
commonMisconceptions: Ordering negatives by magnitude (−5 placed as greater than −2)
Comparing fractions and decimals by surface features instead of converting to a common form
Confusing < and > direction (the 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic misapplied)
Treating ≤/≥ as identical to </> and missing the equality case
Assuming a longer decimal or larger denominator is automatically larger/smaller

learn.summary: For ages 11–12: order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions on a single number line (leftmost = least), and use =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ to compare values, including negatives and mixed representations. The core principle is that POSITION on the line — not sign, digit count, or denominator size — is the single rule that orders every kind of number, and that equal values (e.g. 0.75 and 3/4) sit at the same point, so neither < nor > holds between them; = is the precise relation, and ≤ and ≥ are also true. The primary activity is a hands-on positional sort of mixed-form cards with a common-form conversion check; supporting activities consolidate symbol conventions, interrogate wrong orderings, and read statements in context.

activities.title: Drop mixed-form numbers onto one number line and choose the symbol between neighbours
feedback: If negatives are ordered by magnitude (e.g. −1.5 written as less than −2, or −2 placed to the right of −1.5): anchor on position — further left = smaller; −2 is left of −1.5, so −2 < −1.5. Reason from where it sits, not from digit size.
If 0.75 and 3/4 are placed at different points or not joined by '=': convert one form to the other (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) and land both on the same point, then compare.
If ≤ is used where = or < is meant, or the inequality opens toward the smaller value: read the statement aloud in words — the open side faces the larger value, and ≤ means 'less than OR equal'.

If a longer decimal or larger denominator is assumed automatically larger: place both on the line to test — e.g. 0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal 0.8 is the larger value, so more digits does not mean larger. (For negatives the extra wrinkle is that −0.8 < −0.75.)
activities.rationale: Ordering mixed forms is decided by position, so letting the learner perform the sort, convert to a common form to check, and attach symbols between neighbours makes the one positional rule visible and surfaces the equal-values-coincide case. Dragging, the decimal-conversion toggle, and stacking of coincident cards are optional interaction examples that make the mechanism concrete; they are not required mechanisms, and their comparative effectiveness over other media is not established by the cited sources.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions and use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
learnerActions: Take a set of mixed cards — 0.75, 3/4, −0.8, −0.75, 7/10, −2, −1.5, 1/2 — and place each at its correct position on a shared number line.
Use a 'show as decimal' conversion (e.g. 3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) to check cross-form values before placing them.
Notice that 0.75 and 3/4 land on the IDENTICAL point and coincide there.
Between each adjacent pair of placed cards, select a symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ and justify the choice.
Confirm that between the two coincident cards the strict symbols < and > (and ≠) are false; = is the most precise choice, and the inclusive ≤ and ≥ are also true because they allow equality.
Deliberately test the surprise case: see that −0.8 sits LEFT of −0.75, so −0.8 is smaller, even though 0.8 > 0.75 for positives — defeating the 'bigger magnitude wins' instinct for negatives.
activities.intendedInsight: Position on the number line (left = less) is a single rule that orders integers, decimals, fractions, positives and negatives uniformly; equal values coincide, so < and > cannot hold between them, while = (and the inclusive ≤, ≥) are true.

activities.title: Consolidate the symbol conventions with true/false and ordering checks
feedback: For '−5 < −2': it is TRUE because −5 is further left on the line than −2.
If ≤ and < are treated as identical: recall ≤ also holds when the two values are equal, so a statement using ≤ can be true for equal values like 2, 2.0 and 4/2 (all equal to 2).
If a sequence mis-ranks negatives or equal forms: re-place the items on a line to check before fixing the symbols.
activities.rationale: Recognition and selection items are a useful consolidation companion for the symbol conventions, best used after the positional meaning is established. These items check and reinforce convention use; they do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering.
sourceClaims: KS3 pupils order positive and negative integers, decimals and fractions and use the symbols =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
learnerActions: Judge true/false statements such as '−5 < −2' and explain the reasoning from position.
Match order statements to the correct symbol from =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥.
Order a mixed-form set smallest to largest as a sequence.
Write a single statement using ≤ that is true for all of 2, 2.0, 4/2.
activities.intendedInsight: Order statements and symbol conventions (including strict vs inclusive) can be applied fluently once positional ordering is understood.

activities.title: Interrogate and repair a wrong ordering in discussion or context
feedback: If the learner cannot say why −5 belongs left of −2: tie '−5 < −2' to temperature — −5°C is colder, so smaller, and sits further left.

If strict and inclusive are confused: have them state in words whether equality is possible for the pair; < needs the values to be different, while ≤ is true both when the first is smaller and when they are equal, so ≤ is the natural choice when equality could hold.
activities.rationale: Dialogue can interrogate a wrong ordering and surface reasoning, and reading statements in context ('warmer / further right') supports interpretation of order statements such as −3 > −7. This complements, rather than replaces, performing the positional sort.
sourceClaims: 6.NS.C.7: understand ordering of rational numbers and write/interpret statements of order such as −3 > −7.
learnerActions: Examine a given ordering that mis-ranks negatives (e.g. −5 placed to the right of −2) and explain why it is wrong, referring to position.
Read comparison statements aloud in context, e.g. '−3 > −7 means −3°C is warmer / further right than −7°C'.
Decide when ≤ would be used instead of < between two values, and say why.
State an inference about relative size from a placement, e.g. which of −2 and −1.5 is smaller and why.
activities.intendedInsight: Articulating WHY an ordering is right or wrong — in words and in real contexts like temperature — reinforces positional reasoning and distinguishes strict from inclusive comparison.

constraints: Order by POSITION on the number line (leftmost is least) so negatives and mixed forms are handled by one rule rather than sign-specific tricks.
Convert mixed representations to a common form (decimal or common denominator) before comparing, and verify by placing on the line.
Introduce ≠, ≤, ≥ explicitly alongside <, >, = and contrast strict (<) with inclusive (≤), making the equality case explicit.

Deliberately bait the 'bigger digit = bigger value' error two ways: with negatives (−5 vs −2, where the larger-magnitude number is smaller; and −0.8 vs −0.75, where −0.8 < −0.75) and with unequal-length positive decimals (0.8 vs 0.75, where the shorter decimal is larger) so the misconception is confronted directly rather than accidentally confirmed.
Recognition/selection items (true/false, matching) check convention use but do not by themselves elicit independent construction of an ordering; use the hands-on positional sort for that.

A static labelled line with forms placed and symbols shown can illustrate a completed ordering but does not let the learner perform the sort or select symbols with feedback; it is a worked-example scaffold, not the full task.

Position-order for this objective is represented along a single line (one dimension), so a third spatial dimension is not needed here; this is a scoped observation about representing order, not a general claim that 3D 'adds nothing'.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were NOT re-fetched. Both cited sources carry verified:false in the row. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Math check: −0.8 < −0.75 (−0.8 is further from zero on the negative side, hence further left); −2 < −1.5; 0.75 = 3/4; 1/2 = 0.5; 7/10 = 0.7. Full order of the 8-card activity set: −2 < −1.5 < −0.8 < −0.75 < 1/2 < 7/10 < 3/4 = 0.75. The smaller 5-item diagnostic answer −2 < −1.5 < 1/2 < 3/4 = 0.75 is consistent for its own set.

Original-row inconsistency: the recommendation names −0.75 as the surprise neighbour but never lists it among the cards (0.75, 3/4, −0.8, 7/10, −2). This was corrected by including both −0.8 and −0.75 so the intended comparison is actually available; the original wording is retained only as an uncertainty note.
The 'alligator eats the bigger' heuristic is listed as a common misconception in the source; it is reframed here as reading the open side as facing the larger value, rather than taught as a mnemonic.

Efficacy/necessity of the hands-on track relative to the consolidation checks, static image or dialogue is not established by the standards documents, which support the objective rather than any medium's superiority.

probeDeeper: Is 0.75 the same as 3/4? Convert one to check, then place both.
On the line, which is further left, −2 or −1.5 — and so which is smaller?
Put the correct symbol between −1.5 and −2, and say why.
When would you use ≤ instead of < between two of these?

errorPatterns.pattern: Orders negatives by magnitude: places −2 to the right of −1.5 or writes −1.5 < −2
errorPatterns.nextMove: Anchor on the number line: further left = smaller. −2 is left of −1.5, so −2 < −1.5. Reason from position.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: On the line −2 sits nearer zero than −1.5, or the inequality between them is reversed.

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot compare across representations: treats 0.75 and 3/4 as different sizes, or ranks 0.75 > 3/4
errorPatterns.nextMove: Convert one form to the other (3 ÷ 4 = 0.75) and land both on the same point; then compare.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: 0.75 and 3/4 are placed at different points, or = is not chosen between them.

errorPatterns.pattern: Misuses the strict vs inclusive symbols, or reverses < / >
errorPatterns.nextMove: Read each statement aloud as words; the open side faces the larger value, and ≤ means 'less than OR equal'.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Uses ≤ where = or < is meant, or opens the inequality toward the smaller value.

responseLevels.gap: Orders negatives by magnitude or cannot equate 0.75 and 3/4; symbols used loosely.
responseLevels.full: Places integers, decimals and fractions (positive and negative) on one line, equates equivalent forms, and uses =, ≠, <, >, ≤, ≥ correctly.
responseLevels.partial: Orders within one representation (or the positives) but slips on cross-form equality or negative ordering.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Give a mixed set: −2, 0.75, 3/4, −1.5, 1/2. Say: 'Place these on a number line and order them smallest to largest. Then put the right symbol between 0.75 and 3/4, and between −1.5 and −2.'
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The set mixes representations (fraction vs decimal for the same value) and negatives, so it cannot be ordered by surface features. Placing them on ONE line and choosing = vs <,> reveals whether the child translates between forms and reasons about negative position rather than digit size.
